course.title: Death
course.about: There is one thing I can be sure of: I am going to die. But what am I to make of that fact? This course will examine a number of issues that arise once we begin to reflect on our mortality. The possibility that death may not actually be the end is considered. Are we, in some sense, immortal? Would immortality be desirable? Also a clearer notion of what it is to die is examined. What does it mean to say that a person has died? What kind of fact is that? And, finally, different attitudes to death are evaluated. Is death an evil? How? Why? Is suicide morally permissible? Is it rational? How should the knowledge that I am going to die affect the way I live my life?

bites.headline: You will die. Now what?
bites.body: One fact is unusually stubborn: your life ends. aBit’s Death path doesn’t flinch from that. It asks what mortality means for persons, time, value, and how to live before the lights go out.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: What’s on the table
bites.body: Is death the end—or only a change of address? Would forever be a gift or a trap? What is dying, exactly? The course splits metaphysics (what we are) from value theory (what makes death bad, and life good).
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Drawing the map
bites.body: Kagan sets the syllabus like a border treaty: philosophical questions about death are in; medical trivia and grief counseling are out. First half: what persons and death are. Second half: whether death is bad—and what follows.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Two halves
bites.body: Metaphysics asks what must be true for someone to die. Value theory asks why that matters. Keep the split in mind; arguments will bounce between them all term.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Treat every later lecture as answering either “What is going on?” or “Why should I care?” If you lose the thread, return to that fork.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: What is a person?
bites.body: Before death can matter, we need a subject. Dualism says you are body plus soul. Physicalism says you are a body—though a body with remarkable powers of thought and action.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Dualism
bites.body: On the dualist picture, something non-physical rides along with the organism. That “soul” is often cast as what thinks, chooses, and maybe survives the corpse.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Notice how each later argument about souls, identity, or immortality quietly picks a side in this fight—or tries to dissolve it.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Invisible posits
bites.body: Why believe in a soul you can’t see? One strategy: inference to the best explanation. We invent unseen furniture when it best accounts for what we already agree happens.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Best explanation
bites.body: If ordinary matter can’t easily explain minds, meaning, or unity of consciousness, dualists say a soul is the cleaner story—debate whether that claim holds.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Ask of every soul argument: what exactly is being explained, and is the soul doing unique work—or just renaming the mystery?
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Enter Phaedo
bites.body: Plato’s dialogue stages Socrates on the day of his death—talking souls while facing his own. Kagan uses it to gather more dualist ammo, especially free will.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Free will lever
bites.body: Dualists often claim: if we truly choose, we can’t be only physical machines. A soul is wheeled in to host that freedom.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Watch whether free will really requires non-physical stuff—or whether the dualist smuggles in a contested picture of choice.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Three premises
bites.body: The free-will argument tightens: (1) we have free will; (2) nothing determined has free will; (3) pure physical systems are determined. Conclusion: we aren’t purely physical.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Determinism
bites.body: If every physical event is fixed by prior causes, and you are only physics, your “choices” look like falling dominoes. Dualists refuse that picture for persons.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: You can reject the conclusion by denying a premise—deny free will, deny that physics implies determinism, or deny that free will needs indeterminacy.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Cartesian cracks, Platonic realms
bites.body: Cartesian soul arguments show wear. Plato offers another metaphysics: besides the changing empirical world, there is a second realm of stable Forms.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Two realms
bites.body: The everyday world is messy and temporary. Forms are the clean, intelligible originals—Justice itself, Equality itself—that minds somehow grasp.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: If Forms aren’t physical, grasping them may require a non-physical grasper. That’s the bridge Plato builds toward soul.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Grasping the Forms
bites.body: If Forms are non-physical, a body alone can’t know them. Plato’s “argument from the nature of the forms” says the soul must be what understands that higher realm.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Argument from the Forms
bites.body: Knowledge of timeless objects seems to demand a knower that isn’t stuck in flesh. Immortality often rides along with that claim.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Ask whether understanding abstract truths really needs a separable soul—or whether brains can track patterns without extra ontology.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Simple things don’t shatter
bites.body: Plato’s “argument from simplicity”: destruction means taking something apart. If the soul has no parts, it can’t be dismantled—so it can’t die that way.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Simplicity
bites.body: A composite can break. A partless soul, on this story, has nothing to unscrew. Immortality follows if that picture is right.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Challenge both claims: Is the soul really simple? And is every destruction a matter of parts coming loose?
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Essential properties
bites.body: Kagan presses simplicity further: changeless, partless, indestructible. Then comes the “argument from essential properties”—what the soul essentially is may rule out death.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Essential properties
bites.body: If life or thought belongs to the soul’s essence, then a “dead soul” is a contradiction—like a square circle—rather than a sad event.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Essential-property moves are powerful—and slippery. Watch whether Plato defines the soul so that immortality is baked in by vocabulary.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Same person tomorrow?
bites.body: Metaphysical key to personal identity: what makes you now the same you later? The soul theory answers: same soul, same person—wherever the body goes.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Soul theory
bites.body: Identity rides on an inner nugget that persists. Bodies may swap; memories may blur; the soul is the ticket that keeps “you” continuous.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: If the soul is undetectable, how do we ever know we’ve got the same one? That epistemic headache drives rival theories next.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Body or biography?
bites.body: Two rivals: the body view ties identity to the same living organism; the personality view ties it to the ongoing pattern of beliefs, desires, memories, and projects.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Personality view
bites.body: You are your psychological profile in motion. Swap brains or upload minds, and identity may travel with the pattern—not the meat.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Science-fiction thought experiments will pressure both views. Notice which intuition you trust when body and personality split.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: The duplication problem
bites.body: If personality can be copied, two later people might share your pattern. Both can’t be uniquely you—so bare psychological continuity looks incomplete.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Branching
bites.body: When one past person “splits” into two equally good continuers, identity talk breaks. Theories need a no-branching clause—or a new question.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Duplication doesn’t just threaten personality theory; it forces every identity story to say what happens when there are too many heirs.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: No branching, then what matters
bites.body: Personality theory is patched: same personality without branching. Similar patches hit other views. Then Kagan shifts: maybe “what matters in survival” isn’t strict identity.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: What matters
bites.body: Care about future experiences continuous with yours—even if metaphysics won’t crown a single identical continuer. Survival-value can peel apart from identity.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: When death debates heat up, ask whether we fear losing identity itself—or losing the goods that a continuer would enjoy.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: From survival to dying
bites.body: Maybe survival means a future someone with a personality like yours. Then the camera turns: what is it to die? Focus falls on bodily and mental functions that mark the moment.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Functions
bites.body: Death isn’t just a calendar date. It’s tied to the collapse of capacities—circulation, respiration, cognition—that keep a person going.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Defining death is partly scientific and partly philosophical: which functions are essential to still being here?
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: When P-functions stop
bites.body: Stopping person-functions looks like death—but sleep and coma are exceptions that force finer distinctions. Then a psychological twist: on some level, nobody quite believes they’ll die.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Disbelief
bites.body: We can recite mortality while living as if the end is always for someone else. That gap between saying and believing will power later ethics and fear.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: A clean definition of death still leaves the human habit of denying it. Both threads matter for the badness of death.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Ivan Ilych’s shock
bites.body: Tolstoy’s Ilych knew death was coming yet never believed it—until illness made mortality personal. Kagan treats him as ordinary: abstract knowledge, concrete denial.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Sudden intimacy
bites.body: Death becomes real when it stops being a statistic and starts being your schedule. That conversion is part of why death feels uniquely bad.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: When we ask why death is bad, notice whether we’re talking about the state of being dead—or the rupture of finally believing it.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Missing the goods
bites.body: On the deprivation account, death is bad because it cuts off the good things life would have continued to offer. Being dead isn’t a painful experience—it’s a comparative loss.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Deprivation
bites.body: You’re worse off by missing future joys, projects, and loves—not by suffering inside the grave. Badness is about lost opportunity.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: If deprivation is the story, earlier death can be worse than later death because more possible goods get canceled.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Prenatal nonexistence & forever
bites.body: If missing future life is bad, is missing life before birth also bad? Nagel, Feldman, Parfit enter. Then the pivot: would immortality actually be desirable?
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Asymmetry
bites.body: Many feel future deprivation hurts while past nonexistence doesn’t. Explaining that asymmetry is a live puzzle for deprivation theorists.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Wanting endless life is not automatic. The next lectures ask under what conditions forever would still be a life worth wanting.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Forever—and what makes life good
bites.body: Would endless life stay desirable under the right conditions? Then: what makes a life worth living at all? Hedonism says pleasure—until the “experience machine” thought experiment pushes back.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Experience machine
bites.body: If you could plug into perfect simulated joys, would you? Many refuse—suggesting we value contact with reality, not pleasure alone.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Your theory of well-being shapes whether immortality looks like paradise or a polished trap.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Containers of value
bites.body: Neutral container theory: life’s value is just the sum of pleasant and painful contents. Valuable container theory: being alive itself adds worth beyond the playlist of moments.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Valuable container
bites.body: Existence isn’t a blank vessel. Merely living may carry value—so death can rob you of the container, not only of what’s inside.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: How you score the container changes how tragic early death looks—and how you weigh immortality.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Death can strike anywhere
bites.body: Ubiquity: death may come at any time, to anyone. Imagine death-free vacations or safe hours—then feel how much of life’s texture is shaped by that constant exposure.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Ubiquity
bites.body: The badness isn’t only deprivation at the end; it’s living under an open-ended threat that can cancel plans without warning.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: The human condition is life followed by death. Valuing that package—or resenting it—will steer how we fear and how we choose.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: When fear makes sense
bites.body: How should thoughts of death shape a life? Fear can be fitting—or confused. Separate fear of dying (the process) from fear of being dead (the state and aftermath).
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Two fears
bites.body: Pain, loss of control, and farewell belong to dying. Annihilation or the unknown belong to death itself. Different remedies fit different fears.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Before judging fear as irrational, name the object. Some fears track real losses; others may dissolve under clearer metaphysics.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Finite time, chosen aims
bites.body: Knowing the story ends, how should you set goals and chase them? Time scarcity isn’t only a mood—it constrains which projects can even be sane.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Time constraints
bites.body: Ambitions that need centuries may be beautiful fantasies. Mortality pressures us toward scaled aims—and sharper tradeoffs.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Quality of life partly depends on matching projects to a mortal schedule instead of pretending you have infinite runway.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Two lenses
bites.body: Suicide is explored under rationality (when ending life could make sense) and morality (when, if ever, it could be justified). Keep the lenses distinct.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Rationality vs morality
bites.body: A choice might be prudent for the agent yet still wrong—or kind yet self-destructive. The course examines both questions without collapsing them.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Graphs of life’s quality over time will appear next; they’re tools for the rationality question, not automatic moral verdicts.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Choosing without a crystal ball
bites.body: More cases and graphs: when might ending life be rational? The hard part is deciding whether to continue when you can’t know how the future quality curve will bend.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Uncertainty
bites.body: Tomorrow’s pain or relief isn’t guaranteed. Rational choice under mortality must weigh unknown upturns, not only today’s trough.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: Even if deprivation and well-being theories are clear, uncertainty about your own future complicates any real decision procedure.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Consequences—and duties
bites.body: Suicide’s effects on the agent and on others matter. Utilitarians may stop there; deontologists ask whether further moral constraints apply beyond outcomes.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Deontology vs utility
bites.body: If only consequences count, the math of harm and benefit decides. If rights or duties count too, some acts may be wrong even when the spreadsheet looks tidy.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

bites.headline: Carry this forward
bites.body: The course closes where it began: death forces metaphysics and ethics into the same room. Your answers reshape how you live the time before it.
bites.attribution_line: Shelly Kagan, Death (Yale University: Open Yale Courses), https://oyc.yale.edu/death/phil-176 (Accessed September 23, 2026). License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA

quizzes.prompt: What does Kagan say the course will emphasize?
choices: How to write a living will step by step.
A history of funeral customs across cultures only.
Clinical procedures for declaring someone dead in hospitals.
Philosophical questions that arise when we contemplate death’s nature.
quizzes.explanation: The opening frames Death as philosophy—metaphysics then value—not medicine or etiquette.

quizzes.prompt: How does physicalism answer “What is a person?”
choices: A person is only an immortal soul with no body.
A person is whatever society labels as such this week.
A person is a legal fiction with no metaphysical claim.
A person is just a body—with a rich set of abilities.
quizzes.explanation: Physicalism rejects an extra soul-stuff; the person is the capable body itself.

quizzes.prompt: What is an “inference to the best explanation” doing here?
choices: Positing unseen things to explain agreed-upon phenomena.
Measuring brain waves to locate the soul organ.
Proving souls by quoting scripture alone.
Defining death legally in every state.
quizzes.explanation: The lecture’s first family of soul arguments works by explanatory inference, not direct sighting.

quizzes.prompt: Why do dualists bring free will into the soul debate?
choices: They argue free will can’t fit a purely physical person, so a soul is needed.
They only care about free will in corporate law.
They use free will to prove the body is immortal.
They think free will is impossible for souls too.
quizzes.explanation: Free will is framed as an objection to pure physicalism that motivates belief in an immaterial soul.

quizzes.prompt: What conclusion does the free-will triad aim at?
choices: Determinism only applies to stars, not brains.
Near-death experiences prove reincarnation.
All animals lack free will entirely.
Humans are not a purely physical system.
quizzes.explanation: From free will + anti-determinism + physical determinism, dualists infer we aren’t only physical.

quizzes.prompt: What key Platonic idea does Kagan highlight here?
choices: Only atoms exist and Forms are illusions.
Souls are identical to left-hemisphere activity.
Death is purely a legal category.
Besides the empirical world, there is a second realm of Forms.
quizzes.explanation: The lecture pivots into Plato’s two-realm metaphysics as setup for soul arguments.

quizzes.prompt: What does the argument from the nature of the Forms claim?
choices: Forms prove the body is immortal by itself.
Non-physical Forms must be grasped by a non-physical soul, not the body.
Forms are physical objects stored in temples.
Only children can know Forms.
quizzes.explanation: Plato links grasp of non-physical Forms to a soul capable of knowing them.

quizzes.prompt: What does Plato’s argument from simplicity say about destruction?
choices: Destruction requires divine permission only.
Only heavy objects can be destroyed.
Anything simple is automatically physical.
To be destroyed, something must have parts that can be taken apart.
quizzes.explanation: Simplicity is used to block the usual path to destruction—disassembly into parts.

quizzes.prompt: What is distinctive about the argument from essential properties?
choices: It claims the soul’s essence includes features that make death impossible for it.
It proves only animals have souls.
It shows Forms are destroyed each evening.
It measures soul weight on ancient scales.
quizzes.explanation: The argument turns on what must be true of a soul by nature, not on empirical survival stories.

quizzes.prompt: On the soul theory, what makes you the same person over time?
choices: Having the same soul.
Wearing the same clothes.
Living in the same city.
Sharing a name on a passport alone.
quizzes.explanation: Soul theory locates identity in persistence of the same soul across time.

quizzes.prompt: What does the personality view treat as the key to identity?
choices: The soul as a glowing orb.
Social security number alone.
A unique ongoing set of beliefs, desires, memories, and goals.
Only DNA sequence with no psychology.
quizzes.explanation: Personality theory identifies persons via continuing psychological profile.

quizzes.prompt: What is the main objection raised against the personality theory here?
choices: Personalities never change at all.
Bodies cannot age.
Memories are always false.
The problem of duplication—two copies can’t both be uniquely you.
quizzes.explanation: Duplication cases show psychological continuity can fork, undermining unique identity.

quizzes.prompt: How is the personality theory revised in this lecture?
choices: Same personality counts only if there is no branching or duplication.
Personality is abandoned entirely for soul theory.
Identity requires identical fingerprints only.
Only body continuity matters forever after.
quizzes.explanation: A no-branching requirement is added so personality continuity can’t fork into two “yous.”

quizzes.prompt: When defining the moment of death, what does Kagan first emphasize?
choices: Whether the person owned property.
Bodily and mental functions crucial to marking death.
Astrology charts for the day of death.
Only the opinion of distant relatives.
quizzes.explanation: The turn to “what is it to die?” begins with the functions that fail at death.

quizzes.prompt: Why isn’t “stopping person-functions” a complete definition of death by itself?
choices: Because death never involves the body.
Exceptions like sleep or coma show temporary non-functioning isn’t always death.
Because functions never stop in living things.
Because only plants have person-functions.
quizzes.explanation: Sleep and coma show we need a more careful account than mere temporary loss of function.

quizzes.prompt: What does Ilych illustrate about typical attitudes toward mortality?
choices: People can know death is coming yet not really believe it until it becomes personal.
Only aristocrats fear death.
Illness never changes how we think about dying.
Everyone constantly meditates on their death date.
quizzes.explanation: Ilych models abstract acknowledgment paired with practical disbelief—until crisis.

quizzes.prompt: According to the deprivation account, why is death bad?
choices: Because funerals are expensive.
Because it deprives you of the good things continued life would bring.
Because being dead feels constantly painful.
Because death increases your future pleasures.
quizzes.explanation: Deprivation locates badness in lost goods, not in an experienced hell of being dead.

quizzes.prompt: After discussing deprivation, what new question does Kagan raise?
choices: How to build cryonics tanks in the lab.
Whether insects fear death.
Whether immortality would be desirable, and under what conditions.
How to rename the course mid-semester.
quizzes.explanation: The lecture moves from badness puzzles into the desirability of living forever.

quizzes.prompt: What challenge does the experience machine pose to hedonism?
choices: It shows machines cannot simulate joy.
It argues immortality is always good.
It proves pleasure is the only good.
It suggests we care about more than pleasure—like real connection to the world.
quizzes.explanation: Refusal to plug in is used against the idea that pleasure exhausts well-being.

quizzes.prompt: How does the valuable container theory differ from the neutral container theory?
choices: It assigns value to being alive itself, not only to life’s pleasant or painful contents.
It denies that pleasure ever matters.
It treats life as worthless in every case.
It claims only pain has value.
quizzes.explanation: Valuable container adds intrinsic worth to living; neutral container tallies only contents.

quizzes.prompt: What does “ubiquity” add to the badness of death?
choices: Death only happens on Tuesdays.
Death may occur at any time and strike anyone—an open-ended exposure.
Only celebrities face sudden death.
Death is rare and always predicted years ahead.
quizzes.explanation: Ubiquity highlights unpredictability and universal exposure, not just the final moment.

quizzes.prompt: What distinction does Kagan emphasize about fear?
choices: Fear that grades will be too high.
Fear of cats versus fear of dogs.
Fear only of public speaking.
Fear of the process of dying versus fear of death itself and what may follow.
quizzes.explanation: The lecture separates dying-as-process from death-as-state when assessing appropriate fear.

quizzes.prompt: What practical question does this lecture press?
choices: How to avoid ever thinking about goals.
How to outsource all choices to chance alone.
How to live as if immortal without reflection.
How to set and pursue goals given that life will certainly end.
quizzes.explanation: Certainty of death becomes a constraint on planning and the quality of a lived life.

quizzes.prompt: What two contexts does Kagan use to explore suicide?
choices: Fashion and cuisine only.
Sports rankings and weather.
Rationality (when it makes sense) and morality (when it can be justified).
Typography and architecture.
quizzes.explanation: The series opens by separating prudential and moral evaluations of ending one’s life.

quizzes.prompt: What complicates decisions about continuing or ending life in this lecture?
choices: You cannot be certain how future life quality will go.
Everyone knows their exact future happiness score.
Graphs make uncertainty disappear completely.
Only other people face uncertain futures.
quizzes.explanation: Uncertainty about future well-being is central to the decision problem.

quizzes.prompt: Besides consequences, what do deontologists say may matter morally about suicide?
choices: Further moral factors—such as duties or constraints—beyond outcomes alone.
Whether the person liked philosophy class.
Only the weather on the day of the act.
Nothing else; only taste in music.
quizzes.explanation: The finale contrasts utilitarian consequence-counting with deontological constraints.

quizzes.prompt: Across the arc—from persons and dualism to deprivation, immortality, fear, and suicide—what is Death ultimately asking you to hold?
choices: How to perform clinical resuscitations in detail.
A survey of campus parking rules.
Whether Yale’s dining halls serve dessert.
What death means for persons, value, and how to live given mortality.
quizzes.explanation: Across dualism, identity, deprivation, immortality, fear, and suicide, the arc is philosophical: what we are, why death matters, how to live.
